prompt: What does oxidation give from primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols?

choices.text: Primary: aldehydes or carboxylic acids; secondary: ketones; tertiary: normally no reaction
Primary: ketones; secondary: aldehydes; tertiary: carboxylic acids
choices.why: The classes are mixed up. Primary alcohols give aldehydes or acids, and secondary alcohols give ketones.

choices.text: Primary: aldehydes or carboxylic acids; secondary: ketones; tertiary: ketones
choices.why: Tertiary alcohols don't normally react with most oxidizing agents.

choices.text: Primary: aldehydes or carboxylic acids; secondary: carboxylic acids; tertiary: no reaction
choices.why: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones.

explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidized either to aldehydes or to carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones, and tertiary alcohols don't normally react with most oxidizing agents.

prompt: Why are chromium-based oxidizing agents such as CrO3 rarely used today?

choices.text: They are toxic and a fire danger

choices.why: They can: sodium dichromate oxidizes 4-tert-butylcyclohexanol to 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone in 91% yield.

choices.text: They reduce alcohols instead of oxidizing them
choices.why: Chromium(VI) reagents oxidize alcohols; the chromium itself is reduced.
Tertiary alcohols don't normally react with most oxidizing agents.

explanation: Primary and secondary alcohols can be oxidized by reagents such as CrO3 in aqueous acetic acid, but chromium-based reagents are rarely used today because of their toxicity and fire danger. The Dess–Martin periodinane is used instead.

prompt: Which reagent is used today to oxidize primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones?

choices.text: KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution, with heating
choices.why: Heating with KMnO4 oxidizes primary alcohols all the way to carboxylic acids; the aldehyde can't usually be isolated.
In the book's example, 1-decanol and CrO3 in aqueous acid give decanoic acid. Chromium reagents are also rarely used today.
NaBH4 is a reducing agent. It turns aldehydes and ketones into alcohols, not the reverse.

explanation: Today, primary and secondary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes and ketones, respectively, using the iodine-containing Dess–Martin periodinane in dichloromethane solution.

prompt: Geraniol, (CH3)2C=CHCH2CH2C(CH3)=CHCH2OH, is treated with the Dess–Martin periodinane in CH2Cl2. What forms?

choices.why: The Dess–Martin periodinane oxidizes a primary alcohol to the aldehyde, and the book's example stops at geranial.

choices.text: An epoxide at one of the C=C bonds, with the –CH2OH unchanged
choices.why: The periodinane oxidizes the –CH2OH group; the C=C bonds are untouched.

choices.text: No reaction, because the C=C bonds protect the –OH group
choices.why: Geraniol is oxidized: it gives geranial in 84% yield.

explanation: The Dess–Martin periodinane oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes. Geraniol, a primary alcohol, gives the aldehyde geranial in 84% yield, with both C=C bonds intact.

prompt: What happens when a primary alcohol is heated with KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution?

choices.text: It gives a carboxylic acid; the aldehyde intermediate is oxidized too fast to isolate
It is oxidized to an aldehyde, which can be isolated in high yield
choices.why: An aldehyde does form, but it is further oxidized too rapidly to be isolated.

choices.text: It is oxidized to a ketone, because KMnO4 moves the oxygen to carbon 2
choices.why: Oxidation doesn't move the oxygen. Ketones come from secondary alcohols.

choices.text: Nothing happens, because KMnO4 oxidizes only secondary alcohols
choices.why: KMnO4 in aqueous NaOH oxidizes both primary and secondary alcohols.

explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidized to carboxylic acids by heating with KMnO4 in a basic aqueous solution. An aldehyde is an intermediate, but it can't usually be isolated because it is further oxidized too rapidly.

prompt: What forms when 1-decanol is treated with CrO3 in aqueous acid (H3O+, acetone)?

choices.why: With CrO3 in aqueous acid, the book's example goes on to decanoic acid (93% yield).
Oxidation doesn't move the oxygen. The –OH of 1-decanol is on carbon 1, so the product's carbonyl carbon is carbon 1.
That would be a dehydration product. CrO3 is an oxidizing agent.

explanation: Primary alcohols can be oxidized to carboxylic acids. 1-Decanol with CrO3 in aqueous acid gives decanoic acid in 93% yield.

prompt: 1-Decanol is oxidized by CrO3 in aqueous acid to decanoic acid in 93% yield. How many moles of decanoic acid would 0.200 mol of 1-decanol give?
The mechanism of alcohol oxidation by the Dess–Martin periodinane or by CrO3 is closely related to which reaction?

choices.why: No carbocation forms. After the alcohol bonds to the oxidant, a reduced I(III) or Cr(IV) species is expelled in an E2-like step.
Alcohol oxidation forms a C=O bond at the alcohol carbon; no aromatic ring is substituted.

choices.text: Hydride addition to a carbonyl group
choices.why: That is carbonyl reduction (Section 17.4), the reverse direction.

explanation: All these oxidations occur by a mechanism closely related to the E2 reaction (Section 11.8). The alcohol first forms an intermediate with the oxidant (a periodinane or a chromate), and then a reduced species is expelled as the leaving group as the C=O bond forms.

prompt: In the Dess–Martin oxidation, the alcohol first reacts with the I(V) reagent to form a new periodinane intermediate. What is then expelled as the leaving group?

choices.why: The iodine is reduced as the alcohol is oxidized, so it doesn't leave as I(V).
That is the leaving group when a Cr(VI) reagent such as CrO3 is the oxidant.
Iodine gains electrons as the alcohol is oxidized, so its oxidation state drops from V to III; it doesn't rise.

explanation: In the Dess–Martin oxidation, the first step is a substitution between the alcohol and the I(V) reagent to form a new periodinane intermediate, followed by expulsion of reduced I(III) as the leaving group.

prompt: When CrO3 oxidizes an alcohol, a Cr(VI) chromate intermediate forms and then expels a reduced Cr(IV) species. By how many units does the oxidation state of chromium drop?
explanation: Cr(VI) → Cr(IV) is a drop of 6 − 4 = 2 units: the chromium gains the two electrons lost by the alcohol as it is oxidized to a carbonyl compound.

prompt: How do biological alcohol oxidations by the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+ work?

choices.text: A base removes the –OH proton, and the alkoxide ion transfers a hydride ion to the coenzyme
The coenzyme transfers a hydride ion to the alcohol carbon
choices.why: That is the reverse process, a carbonyl reduction by NADH or NADPH.

choices.text: The alcohol forms a chromate intermediate that expels a reduced Cr(IV) species
choices.why: That is the laboratory oxidation with CrO3.

choices.text: The C–O bond of the alcohol breaks to give a carbocation, which the coenzyme accepts
choices.why: No carbocation forms; the alkoxide ion gives up a hydride ion.

explanation: Biological alcohol oxidations are the opposite of biological carbonyl reductions. A base removes the –OH proton, and the alkoxide ion transfers a hydride ion to NAD+ or NADP+. An example is the oxidation of sn-glycerol 3-phosphate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate, in which the hydrogen is added to the Re face of the NAD+ ring with pro-R stereochemistry.

prompt: Which alcohol gives acetophenone, C6H5COCH3, on oxidation?

choices.why: This primary alcohol would give an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid, with the carbonyl at the end of the chain.
Benzyl alcohol is primary and has one carbon fewer; it can't give a ketone.
Tertiary alcohols don't normally react with oxidizing agents.

explanation: Acetophenone is a ketone, so it comes from a secondary alcohol with the –OH on the carbon that becomes C=O: 1-phenylethanol (Exercise 17.7.1).

choices.why: This tertiary alcohol doesn't normally react with oxidizing agents.
This secondary alcohol gives a ketone, 2-butanone.
This primary alcohol gives butanal, which has an unbranched chain.

explanation: 2-Methylpropanal is an aldehyde, so it comes from oxidation of a primary alcohol with the same carbon skeleton: 2-methyl-1-propanol (Exercise 17.7.1).

prompt: What forms when 2-hexanol is oxidized with the Dess–Martin periodinane?

choices.why: The carbonyl forms where the –OH was, on carbon 2, so the product is a ketone, not an aldehyde.
Only primary alcohols can be oxidized to carboxylic acids. 2-Hexanol is secondary.

choices.text: No reaction, because secondary alcohols resist oxidation
choices.why: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones. It's tertiary alcohols that don't normally react.

explanation: 2-Hexanol is a secondary alcohol, and the Dess–Martin periodinane oxidizes secondary alcohols to ketones: 2-hexanone (Exercise 17.7.2).

prompt: How many of these five alcohols would be oxidized to a ketone: 2-hexanol, cyclopentanol, 1-butanol, 2-methyl-2-propanol, and 1-phenylethanol?
explanation: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones: 2-hexanol (→ 2-hexanone), cyclopentanol (→ cyclopentanone), and 1-phenylethanol (→ acetophenone). 1-Butanol is primary (aldehyde or acid), and 2-methyl-2-propanol is tertiary (normally no reaction).
